Explore / Are reforms and payment infrastructure turning into access, use, quality and outcomes?

A reform can be real before its outcome is known.

Recent reforms are documented at the rule, funding and institution stages: consumer-protection instructions announced in August 2023, a signed 2025 mobile e-money amendment, the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) approved in June 2025, and 2026 steps to build payment institutions. Evidence that they have changed access, use, service quality or outcomes is not yet available. This resource separates rule, funding, institution, implementation, operation, use, quality and outcome, shows the furthest stage the evidence supports for each reform, and leaves every later stage open until it is measured.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
How numbers are presented

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

What reform evidence does not establish

A rule does not prove implementation quality. A funded or procured component does not prove operation. A new institution does not prove adoption. A complaints architecture does not prove effective redress. Participation in a literacy activity does not prove capability. A target does not prove achievement. And missing downstream outcome evidence is not evidence that the reform failed.

Where the reform evidence chain breaks

The biggest gaps sit after formal or implementation milestones: go-live evidence and subsequent active rail use, service reliability, consumer complaint volumes and outcomes, provider compliance in practice, user awareness and capability, and comparable user-level outcomes. Those gaps determine how far each reform can be interpreted.

01
System context

Each stage of the reform chain needs its own evidence

This resource uses one transmission chain, from rule or funding to implementation or institution, operation, reachable access, actual use, quality and protection, and outcome. Each reform is placed at the furthest stage the evidence supports. Missing downstream evidence does not mean the reform failed; it means the later stage is not yet established.

02
Analysis

Official guidance describes a complaint path; performance is unmeasured

A 2024 consumer-protection brochure from the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) describes a provider complaint stage of up to 10 business days, possible extension under stated conditions, and escalation to the central bank within 14 business days. The legal text of the Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions, announced on 28 August 2023, has not been extracted here. Separately, the 2023 mobile e-money instructions set a 10-business-day maximum for complaint processing and require a complaint register. What remains open is actual complaint volume, resolution time, outcome quality, enforcement and consumer experience.

03
Evidence

The e-money amendment changes rules, not observed usage

The signed 2025 mobile e-money amendment permits specified foreign-currency e-money alongside YER and sets transaction and balance ceilings. Those are legal permissions and limits. They do not establish that a provider launched the product, that customers adopted it, what balances are held or how transactions are distributed.

04
Analysis

FPS, RTGS and access support are different parts of the payment-infrastructure reform

The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) separates three functions: a Fast Payment System (FPS), which the project supports in areas under the internationally recognized government; a Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS), to be managed by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) alongside a core-banking upgrade; and a separate access-and-use component covering access-point mapping, capacity building, merchant onboarding in underserved areas and outreach. The project links RTGS to large-value payments between financial institutions, while the FPS is the fast electronic-payment component. The 2026 sequence then adds a CBY-Aden board decision on what the source calls a national QR standard and e-wallet interconnection, unified-network integration work, and the establishment and governance of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). These are different kinds of step — project design, architecture decision, integration and institution-building. None by itself proves go-live, reliability, user adoption, transaction coverage or an inclusion effect. The project’s results framework also records January 2025 baselines for its own project-defined indicators: 817 financial access points (2030 target: 1,021), 1,062,441 active bank accounts (200,898 of them owned by women), 375,252 active e-wallet accounts, 170 merchants accepting electronic payments and 65 agents of licensed financial institutions. These are project baselines that count access points, accounts, merchants and agents — not people — and they have not been reconciled with CBY-Aden’s payment-report totals or with survey measures of account ownership.

05
Regulatory evidence

Adopting a rule and implementing it are different stages, each needing its own evidence

The Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) announced its Financial Consumer Protection Regulatory Instructions on 28 August 2023. That establishes a documented regulatory action. It does not by itself establish provider compliance, supervisory effectiveness, consumer experience, or implementation across all relevant institutions and geographies.

Analysis

Financial-literacy activity is an output until capability is measured

Global Money Week records of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) document activity during 2023–2025. Population financial capability is a different evidence class. Without a suitable baseline, endline or evaluation, this resource does not attribute capability levels or changes to those activities.

Evidence

The July 2026 SMP agreement is staff-level and conditional

On 16 July 2026, IMF staff and Yemeni authorities announced staff-level agreement on policies and reforms that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program. The IMF stated that the agreement was subject to Management approval and would not result in Board discussion. It is not an IMF financing arrangement and should not be presented as Executive Board approval.

Analysis

Funding stages must be kept distinct when reading reforms and programmes

Pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are not interchangeable. A project target is likewise not an observed result. This resource labels the stage of each amount so that commitments, inputs and outputs do not become one cumulative total or an inclusion outcome by presentation alone.

Evidence Readings on this question

Evidence Reading

When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?

A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced.

Evidence Reading

The payment arrived. What happened next?

Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments.

What measurement would change the decision?

Active and repeat digital use

Provider/rail administrative data with deduplication rules and/or demand-side active-use measures.

This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use.
Open this measurement priority

Consumer experience and redress outcomes

Complaint and redress data from providers and the regulator, plus consumer-side evidence on experience, including fees, disclosure and trust.

This evidence would allow redress performance and service quality to be assessed rather than inferred from the existence of rules.
